Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The work is framed around utility-focused research questions about spatial awareness tools (SATs) for visually impaired players, and the game Dungeon Escape is created explicitly as a testbed to evaluate four SAT approaches, not as an entertainment product reappropriated later. The tools are implemented based on prior SAT research, iterated and polished to best represent these utilitarian approaches, with pilot testing to ensure soundness. Disabled stakeholders (visually impaired team members) are involved as part of the research team to refine tool designs, but the primary driver is the utilitarian mechanic of spatial awareness support and its evaluation, not co-creation of a fun-first game. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design where primary utilitarian mechanics are designed and optimized first, with any fun elements secondary.

        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),

reasoning: The study uses a 3D adventure game (Dungeon Escape) where a single participant plays levels, traverses dungeons, and uses spatial awareness tools in real time. There is no indication of discrete turns, phases, or constrained action windows; actions appear continuous and freely timed within the level, which best matches an entirely simultaneous, real-time style rather than any turn-based or phased structure.
